newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African peacekeeping force is necessary, official.
newsitem.headline: African peacekeeping force is necessary, official.

text.p: Prospects for an African peacekeeping force remain distant amid a growing consensus that such a force should have no foreign involvement if formed, South Africa's chief of defence forces said on Monday.
General George Meiring told Reuters in an interview that increased military cooperation between southern African nations would be a prerequisite to the formation of such a force.
Meiring, on a four-day official visit to Tanzania to discuss bilateral defence cooperation, said an African peacekeeping force must be independent of any foreign influence.
"If there is such an animal" it would be an all-African enterprise, he said.
Meiring, quoting Zimbabwe's defence minister, said: "You must have a force out of Africa, for Africa or out of SADC for SADC and not out of the initiative of a foreign power."
SADC -- the 12-nation Southern African Development Community -- is a regional economic and political grouping of southern African nations.

"What we're doing now is trying to get to know one another better, train together perhaps, get the same doctrines, be on the same understandable level about peacekeeping -- and then put a force together if it is necessary to do it," Meiring said.
Defence analysts said any African peacekeeping force would be heavily dependent on South Africa for logistical back-up.
South Africa has the most modern, best equipped and well trained military force on the world's poorest continent wrought with bitter civil wars and internal conflicts.
On Friday, South Africa announced it would send 1,250 troops to Zimbabwe for training in what national television called a first step towards a regional peacekeeping force.
The television said the training was part of a plan to form a multinational peackeeping force under the auspices of SADC.
South Africa said last week it had trained two battalions to be ready for multinational peacekeeping and would be willing to contribute up to 1,000 men to any such operation it approved.

The United States has led campaigns for a "Made in Africa" peacekeeping force but Africans, led by South Africa and Kenya, oppose such a force unless command and control fell totally in African hands.

African nations under the auspices of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) have long championed the idea of a peacekeeping force to end civil wars on the continent but have been hindered by lack of funds.
The OAU faces severe financing problems mainly because of non-payment of dues by cash-strapped member states.
The OAU came under pressure to act on the issue of a peacekeeping or intervention force after it was widely criticised for not making proper efforts to end ethnic wars in Somalia and Rwanda.
Africa's latest war in Zaire now stands out as the greatest challenge to the continental body.

Civil wars have caused massive suffering and wreaked havoc on the economies of several African nations in the last three decades, helping to make the continent the world's poorest despite its immense natural resources and commodities.
